contributions.headingText: Cowden syndrome (CS), also known as PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome (PHTS), is a heterogeneous group of disorders with autosomal dominant inheritance caused by germline mutation of the PTEN gene, characterized by multiple hamartomas and a predisposition to cancer.
LD2D.Y Other specified phakomatoses or hamartoneoplastic syndromes – Cowden syndrome
Acceptable: multiple hamartoma syndrome; PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome.
CS involves organs derived from any of the three germ layers.

CS is characterized by mucocutaneous lesions (multiple facial trichilemmomas, acral keratoses, papillomatous papules, and mucosal lesions are considered pathognomonic), an increased cancer risk, benign hamartomatous overgrowth of tissues (including hamartomatous / juvenile gastrointestinal polyposis), and macrocephaly {24136893; 28476234}. Diffuse oesophageal glycogenic acanthosis in combination with colonic polyposis may be diagnostic of CS {21437855; 23238744}. Cancer risk is relatively widespread, including risk for breast, thyroid, endometrial, renal cell, and colon cancers, as well as melanoma {20301661; 28476234}.

PHTS also includes Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba syndrome and Proteus syndrome. However, most PHTS cases correspond to CS, and these terms are often used interchangeably {19668082}.

The prevalence has been estimated at about 1 case per 200 000–250 000 individuals in a European population. This may be an underestimate given the difficulty in diagnosing this syndrome {10234502}. Female CS patients have a cumulative lifetime breast cancer risk (to the age of 70 years) as high as 85% and a relative risk of 25 {22252256; 20565722}. Multifocal and bilateral breast cancer has been reported in 34% of CS patients with breast cancer {20565722; 28476234}. Male CS patients are also at increased risk of breast cancer, although the exact magnitude of risk is unclear {11238682; 28476234}. Benign breast lesions can be found in the majority of female CS patients {9445133}.

CS is an autosomal dominant disorder with age-related penetrance and variable expression. Germline mutation in PTEN (10q23.3) is found in about 85% of CS cases, as well as in subsets of other PHTS disorders (65% in Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba syndrome, 20% in Proteus syndrome, and 50% in Proteus-like syndrome) {19668082; 18794875; 9140396; 8673088}. Individualized risk calculation may aid in the assessment of a patient’s risk of carrying a germline PTEN mutation on the basis of clinical features {21194675}.

Germline SDH mutations have been found in about 5% of patients with PTEN mutation–negative CS/CS-like phenotypes, and they are associated with increased frequencies of breast, thyroid, and renal cancers beyond those conferred by germline PTEN mutation {18678321}.

PTEN, which is a virtually ubiquitously expressed tumour suppressor, is a dual-specificity lipid and protein phosphatase that regulates cell proliferation, cell migration, and apoptosis through inhibition of AKT via the PI3K/AKT pathway {23613428}. Inactivation of the second copy of the gene allows deregulation of the AKT pathway.

Benign breast pathologies occur in about 75% of female CS patients and include ductal hyperplasia, intraductal papillomatosis, adenosis, lobular atrophy, fibroadenomas, and fibrocystic change. Many patients show features suggestive of a breast hamartoma. Malignant breast lesions are mostly invasive carcinoma of no special type (NST), often associated with ductal carcinoma in situ {9445133}. A recent report suggests that apocrine differentiation is common in breast cancers from patients with germline PTEN mutations, and expression profiling puts these cancers in the molecular apocrine category {20712882}.
The International Cowden Consortium (ICC) operational diagnostic criteria are listed in #1604 Box 9.01 .
Patients with PHTS are at increased risk of several types of cancer, and interval screening is recommended (see #1605 Table 9.04) {22252256; 23613428; 23335809}.
